projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Spero W. Calos was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: First thing I'd like you to do is tell us your name and spell your last name.

sp.speaker: Spero W. Calos
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Go ahead.

sp.speaker: Spero W. Calos
sp.p: Right now?

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Spero W. Calos
sp.p: My name is Spero W. Calos. Calos with a C. C-A-L-O-S. I was born in Kenmare, North Dakota, however, my relatives moved through Duluth, Minnesota, what seemed to be the congregating point of all those people coming from Greece, and then my family, my father and mother, moved down to Tarpon Springs, Florida, and then from there, we went to a farm in Palmetto so I'm a farm boy, grew up in Palmetto, Manatee County, Florida.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Well, why in 1938 did you get involved in the military?

sp.speaker: Spero W. Calos
sp.p: Okay. If you know the economic conditions in those days, the government gave you, when you got into the National Guard, and I started at 16 years of age, and that was permissible, however, when the war was declared, all those under 16, or under 18, were not evicted but discharged because they weren't allowed, before the war it was legal but after the war -- but it was a dollar and 15 cents drill, for about an hour and a half's pay, at night. Monday night. Today, when you have a weekend drill, it's a Saturday Sunday affair, but those days, it was a dollar 15 cents.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Tell us a little bit about the training that the National Guard went through before the war.

sp.speaker: Spero W. Calos
sp.p: Okay. All right.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: What kind of equipment did you have?

sp.speaker: Spero W. Calos
sp.p: All right. First, you come through and the 38, we had the 1903 rifle, which was used in World War II. It wasn't until World War II started we got the M-1, but we trained and of course, you do your basic training, you are in the close order drill and all the requirements then and then you learn all of the basic other requirements: The sanitation, map reading, all those things required to be an accomplished soldier when you're in the field. Now, every summer, we would go to summer camp, which is the same way they do now. We usually would go up to Camp Blanding, Florida, and it was sort of a fun period, but it was also laborious and doing all the training, the night maneuvers, marches, nothing to march many miles with one quart of water, and this is a type of training. Now, I was in a regular line out there. A line, for those that don't understand, means a regular infantry outfit that we had the basic weapons 03 at that time, and then you had the 60-millimeter mortar, and then we had the 81 millimeter mortar. Then you also had what we had was the light machine gun, it was 30 caliber, but it's air cooled as opposed to the water cooled which you have water cooled machine guns in every company out of four companies in a battalion. IKM, which is milk, the battalion I was in, I was in I Company 124 at that time before I got to the 167th here. And the M Company was the one that had the heavier mortars and air cooled machine guns, and of course they were utilized to reinforce the infantry companies. This is the basic training that you did there, and you'd learn the different -- right off the head, I can't think of -- there are a million and one different things you have to learn: Sanitation, road -- what did I say, map reading and things of this nature. Learning how to operate the guns.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: So when Pearl Harbor happened, you had been in the National Guard for almost a year?

sp.speaker: Spero W. Calos
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: So tell us how you heard about Pearl Harbor back and where you were and what your thoughts were.

sp.speaker: Spero W. Calos
sp.p: Just to give you an idea, on that weekend, I was on leave from Camp Blanding. All right. In the meantime, the unit was federated. In 19 -- November 1940, November '40. December 7, '41, so it was a year before they federated and took us to Camp Blanding. So on the weekend of Pearl Harbor, before I went home, and I was on my way home, believe it or not, in those days, you could hitchhike -- and Tampa, Florida, when the Japanese bombed Pearl Harbor, and of course we come back and then training became intensified. Camp Blanding was being constructed. They were building the water tank that hadn't been completed. So we were in six-man hutmans so it was kind of rustic, and this is the type of training we had. Now, I don't know to what extent we are and how long we are to last here but --

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: About ninety minutes. Have that much?

sp.speaker: Spero W. Calos
sp.p: Well, I probably, well, to give you an idea now, because in my period of time, we had what they call a square division. Do you have any military?

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Well, you know --

sp.speaker: Spero W. Calos
sp.p: You got a regular division now, 3 regiments what they call brigades now, but in those days, we had four regiments. Two regiments was a brigade, hence the term brigadier general. Two regiments, brigadier general. They comprise the division. They felt that wasn't aerodynamic and like the German contact and aggresiveness and they pulled the 24 that I'm with and they sent us to Ford Bening, Georgia, as school troops to try to militarize the Dixie division. So for approximately a year and a half, we were school troops with the 24th, as I played football there, yeah, played on the football team and and that was enjoyful.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Can you take a minute and describe what it means to be a school troop? A lot of people don't understand what that means.

sp.speaker: Spero W. Calos
sp.p: Okay. Fort Bening was also a jump center, the jump center is where the people learn to become paratroopers, and I used to envy them at that time but they wouldn't allow us at that time because now the school has been transferred to Fort Bragg is where the jump center is now. 8:16 But then, it was centers for specialized weapons, the weapon, the machine machine guns, at this time -- ones were starting to come about, tactics, and then an important part of training, you learn how to do all that stuff, then you have to have basic training, and then you have basic advanced, and then you have super advanced training, and that's where we did a lot of that heavy mortar, and I think about we never had it as bad as it was if you've done any of the civil war when one outfit had to go and say, gee, take these troops from one place to another and the only way they could get there was by walking. Well, we had a little of that. Of course, in our element, it wasn't as fierce as it was then but you learned water discipline. You learned how to protect your feet, blisters, how to rest at night and things like that. This was the learning of a basic infantryman.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: What comes after Fort Benning for you?

sp.speaker: Spero W. Calos
sp.p: All right. Fort Benning, finally, the war is progressing, right? So what do they do? Moved us back to keep in mind now the 124th is no longer, is dissolved, that regiment. 10:07 So then they send us back, and I went to 167th, Dixie division, and that's the one that I listed here, and that's the one that I stuck with all the time.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Was the division already deployed or were they still in Florida?

sp.speaker: Spero W. Calos
sp.p: They were still in Florida, yeah, but then, I continued the training. We marched, I remember one time we marched all the way from Blanding to Ocala, 60 miles, and then we marched back; of course we did it in incremental days, but we'd march a day, we'd walk, pull off, set up the pup tents in a bivouac. But then, came time to ship out. So we didn't know where in the world we were going to be sent, you know? And we could grasp that we're getting no woolen material, it was all -- so eventually, the word eked out, you're going into the south Pacific. So they then started us to ship out. Of course, the first place we went from there to camp -- and then more or less a staging area, make sure your hair was almost shaven back, you had the necessary shots, all there. Then we went to H -- and got on a Dutch freighter that had been converted into a ship. There were six bunks about this high, and you had about that much between each bunk. The ship was an NS something, I have trouble remembering this today but I'll never forget that Dutch ship, called Coda Enta, I don't know what it means but some Netherlands type of name. And that's where we got on there, Norfolk. Rode on from Norfolk all the way down and keep in mind that's when I got sick going down to Panama canal. The Atlantic ocean was fierce. And then we went through the locks at Panama, and got into you know how locks are, it's by height because the two are not level and cargo way they went through during Teddy Roosevelt's time to make the canal goes through those locks but then when you get to the last area, got Katoon Lake before you get into the ocean and there was announcement comes out on the PA system that says, if you want fresh water shower, this is your chance to do it because you won't have a chance again cause Katoon Lake was fresh water. But because after that, salt water, even then you only had a certain amount of water which was rationed. It took us 37 days to go. From Panama Canal and the first place to go was Good Enough Island. But then after three or four days, they got the change of orders, you go to not New Guinea how can you like a parallelogram, you know, what a parallelogram type of island and if we take eastern portion of it there, little place called right in there is called Moro is it, more or less.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Port Moresby?

sp.speaker: Spero W. Calos
sp.p: Thank you. Port Moresby. No, we didn't go into Port Moresby, we went near there, a little place called Ora Bay, O-R-A Bay and they had skeletonized an area for us to be there because it is not combat and we had to set up some sort of tents, and then immediately when we came out, the roll call and everybody come to roll call bring your canteens with water. And the tender in the platoon leaders had to supervise you in order to make sure your Atabrin. Atabrin replaced quinine because quinine was not available at that time, consumption or the amount of quinine was in possession of the Japanese but the scientists got atabrin and -- 15:33

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: What was the atabrin for?

sp.speaker: Spero W. Calos
sp.p: I'm sorry, I'm thinking myself, without a doubt: Malaria. Well, I thinking ahead. I took it for granted.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: I know what it --

sp.speaker: Spero W. Calos
sp.p: Well, no, because they -- sure. Where did we leave off there? Out of breath.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: We were talking Oro Bay so just pick it up from ORO Bay and talk about going on. Go ahead.

sp.speaker: Spero W. Calos
sp.p: Okay. When when you're there, you got to learn protection for how to protect yourself against the malaria and you could not, you had to wear your shirts and in most cases, you had to wear a long sleeve when advisable. A lot of times we didn't but that was necessary, and then they had to take the environment surrounding that area to ensure that you could eradicate the mosquito. Learn, had to go through the anophalies mosquito, you go through their stage, the live cycle, the pupa, the larva and then the adult. You had to learn all of that and take care of yourself that way. And I remember we had to go around, and any stale water, we had to film a layer of oil over it in order to kill the larva. Yeah, the larva is the one that comes up and last a little pipe, a little and he sticks it in the water that's how he breathes, and then of course you suffocate them but we learned about that. Then we learn to put on not jump boots, I'm thinking, in fact, the second, not jump boots but jungle type of boots that are feasible and usable in this forest, in a very jungle area. And then we were there for about two and a half three months. By this time, you could look at your skin and you were getting yellowish from the Atabrin. And then from there, we went on our first encounter combat. Then, now keep in mind, the island of New Guinea. Now, if we come up to the northern coast, sort of a diamond shaped like I said or like a parallelogram here, and take the northern coast, and then we went, hedge hopped, going line LAE was one island, Hilandia, Wakee Island, you come in with LCI, landing craft infantry, you'd come in. We did have sporadic fire but nothing like D-Day or anything like that they had in Europe. But if and this is what you would do, you would do that and stay this for a week, two weeks or whatever it necessary, and then go to the next one. But now let's go back to Ora Bay. North of Ora Bay is a place called Boona. Okay. How we got there, I don't know exactly but it was two or three months or a little around that time that the Boona campaign entered. And of course, the people listening in here will know that that is the southern most point that the Japanese acquired or contacted and attacked before being repelled, and I don't know the outfit but I'm thinking it's the 32nd division that, the one that caught, to put it bluntly, hell, and they took quite a beating there. But from there on, then we did all of the other islands. Many times, when we'd pull into an island, you'd go in about, oh, about a half a mile, sometimes less than that, and you'd set up a perimeter around there, dig trenches, and that's where you'd stay overnight. 20:28 And we're sending patrols out ahead, come back, day patrols. Go out, come back to see if you could make contact with the enemy. Then alternate days, we were allowed to walk back, and we were at the beach, go to the beach and certain times, go swimming. Then they pull in and then they say, okay, you'd pack and then you'd go to your next place. Zanzipor is the northwestern most point of New Guinea where we went, and we stayed there setting up patrols, getting ourselves prepared. Now, very interesting, but very, what shall I say, uncalamatous event: The regimental commander and Sansipor Zanzipor was a little strip, air strip, so the regimental commander had called in and says he wants all the battalion commanders -- no, no, he wants all the company commanders, because we are only a battalion size then, because you don't fight in jungle warfare like you do in Europe connecting with your outfit on the right and left. Here, it's individual, and you go on your attack that way, and then when you bunk in for the night, you set up a perimeter like the old, shall we say, wagon days. 22:18 Well, the commander wants all the company commanders to report to the airport, and at that time, our company commander, Leonard -- Captain White, was, believe it or not, ill, critically ill, and he couldn't be there so he sent a second lieutenant. He was in charge of the weapons platoon, and he went there. So the plane, they went, gathered up and took off at the airport and out to check Japanese supply lines. Go into the interior of the -- what's the name of the island, what's the name of the mountains?

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Holy Stanley mountains?

sp.speaker: Spero W. Calos
sp.p: See, I forgot. Holy Stanley Mountains. To check those paths along the way. Would you believe that night came, ended, and he didn't come in. The next day, he didn't come in. About three days later, Lieutenant Wile came walking up the coast, the only survivor. They had crashed, and he managed to make it back. All the other company commanders plus the battalion commander plus the regimental commander. The regimental commander was a westpointer Colonel Mendenhall. I remember him because he made several speeches before so it was unfortunate circumstance. From there, we okay --

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Before you move on, can you kind of give us first impressions of a jungle fight? You talked a little bit about it. Talk about how much you could see, what kind of encounters you had with the Japanese, and those sorts of things?

sp.speaker: Spero W. Calos
sp.p: Just as you have a pistol, not a pistol, just as you have a rifle, as a weapon, you had a machete. A machete was a vital instrument needed in cutting away territory. Okay. What you would do, you had to have a compass and you'd shoot cause you'd know from the map, you couldn't see in front of you like they say you couldn't see 30, 40 feet in front of you because of the jungle fare so you would know a general cut as matter in the general direction and then march on. Well you'd have two men in front of you, and two men which are scouts in front of the platoon, or whatever the unit was, and this is where you'd cut right on through. 25:05 I remember one time we went in, we had heard some Japanese, we had gone into the interior, and we heard the Japanese, and they sent the word back, believe it or not, they had not heard us, and we remained quiet, and the sun of a guns came right into us, and we through a barrage at them and I do remember that. And we just slaughtered them. It was a small group, but they had they had their little gardens out there and everything. But you cannot see in front of you, and it's just you had to fight your way through with machete when you were penetrating the jungle area, and then as I mentioned, you then, every night you had to dig your foxhole, make a circular perimeter, put your weapons, your mortars in the center, and this is the way we did it. 26:07

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: So what was the worst enemy, the Japanese or the terrain?

sp.speaker: Spero W. Calos
sp.p: Well, I would say probably the terrain because we had sporadic -- we lost a few men, believe it or not, I looked up and you have a device there at the center that you have here, it's not here, it's more toward the, what did we refer to --

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: The memorial?

sp.speaker: Spero W. Calos
sp.p: The memorial, where you put man's last name, first initial, first name. And I pulled Frank High's name just like that. Company A67 division where the person that passed away.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: He is one of the guys in your unit that was lost?

sp.speaker: Spero W. Calos
sp.p: Yes. Lost. Yeah Wilkison. We lost several.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: What kind of fights were they where you lost these guys?

sp.speaker: Spero W. Calos
sp.p: Just snipers. Snipers. And as I mentioned, any time you go on a patrol, you send two men in front of you, one in front of the other, and then the main body below. And this is the way you would go. You take your breaks, you'd send words, messages, up and down, and this is the way we did it that way. And to advance that element, just to give you an idea, when we went from Sansipor, we went to Morotai. Morotai is at that time, it was not Indonesia, it was Dutch -- what do you call it?

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Dutch East Indies?

sp.speaker: Spero W. Calos
sp.p: Dutch East Indies. And Morotai was one of the larger islands but very small compared to the Halmaheras which are much larger islands that 40,000 Japs was on there and a very strategic move on MacArthur's part. We just leapfrogged them. And then very limited, we killed a few Japs right there and no one got hurt, and I remember as we were penetrating through and went to wherever our furthest point, then when we pulled back in a couple days, those Japs were still there and had started deteriorating. Nobody had taken any steps to bury them or anything like that. So we stayed very short time at Morotai. From Morotai, we made another quick landing on the island, and then we went to the second largest island, Mindinao. Luzon is the main island where Manila, the capital, and then the southern most, one of the southern most islands and the second largest is Mindinao. Codabato are the cities, Davao in there. Again, we made our invasion there with very little effort until we got into the hinterlands, and you'd go up these ridges, and this is where I was going to say, mention a little while ago: When you set your line, you know, and here you are, independent, you're on a ridge, nobody on the right and left, and you got your scouts out in front of you, got the main body behind you, this one particular time, the company, the first sergeant came up and he was pressing word, he says that word come from battalion, "cease all acts of aggression." What the hell they mean by that? He says something about they dropped an atomic bomb, and that's all you heard of it. And then from that, the gossip got louder and louder. We stayed there for about a day, and we turned around and went back to the flatland, set up our camp there in order to receive instructions. And then our purpose was to accept the surrender of the Japanese who were in the mountains. Now, we're still in Mindinao. We had gone, we had gone from Cotabato but then we moved, we walked over until we got to, I don't know whether we had to take LCI's or not to come back over Davao, and Davao is where we set up our camp. Our battalion set up 17 camps. A camp was about large enough, a camp was about 14 acres. Now, I know what 14 acres is cause we used to have a 14-acre patch, I grew up on a farm. It's, how else can I say it, it's about 50 yards, about 50 yards wide, and about maybe 100 yards deep. And there, one thousand bodies there. When we were ready to take soldiers, to take family, civilians, to take different types of persons, and then they would have, we'd set up and have our trucks that would give, issue just like we have a mess hall, you know, at camps, and behind the service company, you know, they serve all the rations and everything, we would serve the basics that we would give them, rice, and this sort of thing, but then each compound had to send 50 men, and they'd come loose and be under one, we had one man with a gun that would go with them and tell them to go to a particular area and they would come back, retrieving edible vegetables, food that they could utilize. 33:00 And they are experts at that because keep in mind now, they had been living with that for several months so they're quite intelligence about that. And this is the way we were there until about three months. The Japanese got to go home before we got home.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: I'm thinking that the guy with the gun wasn't there to watch the Japanese but to protect them, is that correct?

sp.speaker: Spero W. Calos
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: How did the Filipinos feel about the Japanese?

sp.speaker: Spero W. Calos
sp.p: Oh, man, very joyous. Nothing like the like we're hearing sporadic, we're hearing the good and the bad, we're hearing the bad in Iraq. They are exceptionally thankful, cooperative. Now, I even remember one thing when we were at Davao, and every night, they would allow us to go into town because by this time, they had a big brassy band, and I remember they had dance girls and everything, and I remember I used to go to the mess hall and get me a container of grapefruit juice and take it with me, and then when you get downtown in Davao, because we were out in the perimeter around there, you get that White Bull, which is a type of, we called it White Bull, type of alcohol, believe it or not, cut it with grapefruit juice and they had these brassy bands and we had a nice time. It was a joyous period. Mental relief. You didn't have that fear when you're on the the jungles. Keep in mind, you're a hardened soldier but you're still afraid. You're still protective. You got to do all around protection, and so much that I've forgotten now because keep in mind, this is over 50 years ago. But those are things that are indelibly printed in your mind that you'll never forget. 35:15 So we stayed there for three months. Believe it or not, we were there, one of our members died, just natural death. Pappy, we used to call him Pappy because he was one of the elderly fellows. He died. We took him back in the ship; he was not thrown overboard. We took him back all the way home and that pretty much --

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Couple of real quick questions.

sp.speaker: Spero W. Calos
sp.p: Anything, anything to fill in.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Well, how did you guys feel about the Japanese? As soldiers as the enemy, how did you feel about them?

sp.speaker: Spero W. Calos
sp.p: We were not very, what shall we say, hindrance to them, not at all. In fact, when we accepted their salute, when they were, you know, surrendered, they were very cooperative, we gave them C rations. No harsh sentiment whatsoever. I don't know whether I've expressed that to you strong enough.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: That's fine. Some guys have some pretty hard feelings about the Japanese.

sp.speaker: Spero W. Calos
sp.p: All right. Now, one field just to give you an idea, let's say this one particular day that I remember was civilians, and when they come to the field, they have to come in, spread themselves out, and then lay a blanket and all their possessions on that. 37:00 And then we'd come and peruse them, look over them, taking anything that we feel like we could, cause I remember a lot of men took some watches, but we didn't bother them too much for that. Now, the weapons were caught, were taken and put into a truck and they moved them away.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: How do you feel about General MacArthur?

sp.speaker: Spero W. Calos
sp.p: Love him. I love him, when I think back. There -- well, let me go back. Well, I was also in Korea, and I was in the 24th division. We were the first ones there. The war ended. Pardon me, the war, the gooks, I call them the gooks, the north Koreans, crossed the parallel June 25, '50. To July, we were in Pusan, and of course there, we went up there and the first contact was in Chonan about halfway up to there at the 38th parallel, and whammo, those T34 tanks and everything hit us so hard, and we went back through through Tejan and Tegu all the way back to the Nectan. I'm leading to a point here. The Nectan is a river around Pusan and that's we stayed. 38:41 The strategy of MacArthur brought those Marines into Incheon right north of Seoul, just south of the parallel. Cracked the nut of the North Koreans just like that. Few days later, they told us march order, and we leapfrogged everyday without contact because the back of the North Koreans was broken. And of course, I think very much of him for that strategy. I think of him very much, though I've heard a lot about him bickering with Nimitz and this and that and MacArthur was a fancy pants. He loved to strut. This was his demeanor. But do you know something, you know how hard it is to go to school and of course if you go to a military school, how hard it is to make good grades? When I think of MacArthur and Lee having gone four years through West Point and never had a demerit, it's remarkable. What other individual could there -- comes Sherman, he had loads of them. So I think very much of him. Very much. He is a strategist. I do believe that. And I hope we have some of that now that can, of course, it's kind of hard to have any definite strategy here.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Well, how about taking a minute and compare the Japanese and the North Koreans as enemies, what were they like?

sp.speaker: Spero W. Calos
sp.p: The Japanese and the North Koreans?

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Yes. What was the difference between fighting the Japanese and fighting the North Koreans?

sp.speaker: Spero W. Calos
sp.p: Oh, I think the North Koreans were more dynamic. Evidently, the way they were trained, the communist trained them there, see, more dynamically, more fierce than the Japanese. We never had that fierceness that I would say that's to the Russians. There's a good article about the Russians in today's, I think it's the Post -- read it -- how they still clinging to the old Stalin methods, but I can vividly remember, like you say, we remember it when we had to bring ourselves back, we were being slaughtered and trying to fight our way back because they had gotten behind us and Tejan was massacre, they just clobbered us. And all the roads in those vehicular, we did have a few vehicles. If they tried to make it out, they were already ambushed so you had to make it back on foot. And on the ridge mountains they're on struggling to get back. 42:22 So I would say, at that point because of that feature that I can compare the North Koreans, the Japanese had inferior, their 25-caliber weapon, rifle, was nothing more than a 22. It would kill you, there is no doubt about it. Far simpler than our 30-caliber weapons. Their mortars were far simpler. The heavier stuff I don't know about it because we never got involved on that, but we never experienced, never experienced other than mortar fire. I don't remember most of the time ever experiencing any Howitzers, anything if they had anything like Howitzers, which they would land on us. But they would land the mortar stuffs because when we had set up a perimeter, I remember one time we had, what do you call it, not a bomb, but a shell landed right near us. You could see the burned area around it.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: You mentioned the, well, let's hold on just a second before I get ahead of myself. Why did you decide to stay in the military after World War II?

sp.speaker: Spero W. Calos
sp.p: Okay, I got out and stayed seven months. I matriculated for the University of Florida, Tallahassee -- no, Gainesville. Gainesville. And I knew that I had to have an education because I went right straight out of high school, keep in mind, right straight out of high school into combat. So I knew I needed an education cause I was competing with Westpointers. Now, I think I was as well qualified for infantry tactics and weaponry as any Westpointer but beyond that, I did not have the education, so I was going to go back. Would you believe I spent my $300 mustering out pay? They gave you a hundred dollars per three months, for 300 mustering out pay for World War II donation. I used that, I didn't have anything. I had still more time to go before September would start with going to school, I turned around and re-upped. Went back into the service for the lack of doing something, and financially. And got into the airborne. Got that extra $50. This time, support my mother, for support, I needed the money. Doesn't sound much now, but it was a lot of money then, so that's why.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Where along the line did you get your commission?

sp.speaker: Spero W. Calos
sp.p: Okay. Along the line, evidently, a regulation came out. Okay, let me set the stage. After World War II, the services were drained of military, and they didn't have enough men to fill up the various out -- mainly the divisions in the foreign lands as well as in the United States. So the government realized that they would allow high school graduates to be commissioned with certain expectations, certain requirements. I got my high school diploma, filled out the other material that they wanted, and went before a board and it's called a presidential citation, not citation, presidential appointment. That's how I got commissioned without a college education. Because when we went back, where did they send me? To the 24th division. Even when Korea broke out, there were only two battalions in the regiment, and they were only about 60 percent filled and you need three regiments. 47:22 There weren't many officers so there was a requirement for personnel, and I grabbed it because I don't think that would happen today. That wouldn't happen today.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: So were you in Japan already on Garrison? What was that like?

sp.speaker: Spero W. Calos
sp.p: Okay. Yeah. Keep in mind, I had a wife then. I got married. I got married in one day, commissioned on the next. 47:50 We went on our honeymoon to Puget Sound, Seattle, and departed with my wife, left her there. We had a car, left her with a car, and I went, sailed. At that time they didn't have the Air Corps or anything like that so we sailed, I sailed, to Japan. Left her. Nine months, we were separated. Then I was assigned to the 34th infantry regiment at Sasebo. Sasebo is the city, naval city, on Kyushu. Kyushu is the southern most island, Honsho being the main one, where Japan, where Tokyo, Yokohama and all of those. There is Chikoko, Hokkaido, there were about five or six major islands. We were on Kyushu and that's where we were on Sasebo which was the second largest naval base for the Japanese next to Yukuska, which was up there near Yokohama. And so it was a direct to Sumi Straits between Sasebo and Pusan. They loaded us up in a ferry and that's where we went. Like I told you second of July, we were there. 49:32 Then yes, we rode planes, we rode buses, trucks, we had trucks for a certain point to get on the trains, and then we rode a train all the way up to a point called Chonan, and I'll always remember that because that's when we first made the contact. And of course, they were already prepared, and they were in real, shall I say, battle gear ready, already prepared. And, man, they clobbered us and we bounced all the way back.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: That's a little bit of a shock, wasn't it?

sp.speaker: Spero W. Calos
sp.p: Oh, a hell of a shock, a hell of a shock. General Dean, would you believe that I saw General Dean. General Dean incidentally was the commander of the division, and I had seen him the night before when he was on a Jeep patrolling around and evidently, after that, he must have run into a trap, and then he got loose, he managed to get loose, and he walked, he went across the field, and they captured him on a mountain, near a mountain side. And of course we didn't know anything about that until he had mentioned it in his biographies later. So that was a shock. 51:15 We lost a hell of a lot of men, and I had just finished -- every year we have a reunion with the battalion that I was in. That is also a division reunion for the 24th Division which will be in Albuquerque, but we also have one for our battalion because we are the ones, we know those men and we have become very familiar and they're just like brothers now, and we just had it in Missouri. What do you call it --

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Branson? 52:00

sp.speaker: Spero W. Calos
sp.p: Branson, Missouri. And we tell our stories there, but we lost a lot of men, lot, quite a few men.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Were you involved when the Chinese came in?

sp.speaker: Spero W. Calos
sp.p: Oh, I think I got hit by Chinese weapon. Okay, we saw them. All right, now when we went up to within our division, went within 14 miles of the Yaloo, the seventh division was on our right, and I think it's the 27th Regiment of the seven was the only outfit that made Yaloo. They made Yaloo. And of course, like I was telling you, we had leapfrogged going like that. One night, when we pull off the road, everyday, you would set up your communication, you had the little twisted telephones like that. They said, load up, and meet the trucks at the road. They had found that the Chinese had intervened, and we had to get out of there right quick so we went to the trucks and rode back hastily to the 38th parallel. And there we stayed, determined what they're going to do. Then they tried to get contact with the nation, United Nations, of course, then the idea was then to make contact with the North Koreans and there it was a seesaw battle until they finally decided that Japan -- after we head back to the 38 parallel, we penetrate a little bit and then they bounce us back and the end was stalemate. And to me, it's regretful that we have 30,000 men still over 50 years on the 38th parallel. Horrible. I understand now they're going to probably pull some of those men out and maybe send them fellows, send them to Iraq because that's where they'll need them. That's sums up everything right from the top of my mind, I hope.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: I think you've done an excellent job. That's great. Well, thanks very much for taking the time.

sp.speaker: Spero W. Calos
sp.p: Okay, it's been a pleasure. And your name? Say it so it'll be on there.

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: I'm Gary Rhay.

sp.speaker: Spero W. Calos
sp.p: Gary Rhay and and you are from?

sp.speaker: Gary Rhay
sp.p: Denver, Colorado.
